t: Minimum Score by Changing Two Elements — Three Removal Candidates
o: Change exactly two elements to any values to minimize (max pairwise difference) + (min pairwise difference) of the resulting array. Since changed values are free, set them equal to some surviving element: the low score becomes 0, so we only minimize the range (high score) of the n−2 untouched elements. The untouched set is everything except two removals; the minimal range is achieved by deleting two smallest, two largest, or one of each. Example 1: sorted [1,4,5,7,8]; delete {7,8} leaves range 8−5 = 3. Example 2: sorted [1,3,4]; deleting two elements leaves one element, range 0.
k: Changed elements can always duplicate a survivor, forcing the low score to 0; only the range of survivors matters.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort and try three deletion patterns
a.i: After sorting, the survivors' range for each deletion pattern is a single subtraction: keep middle after dropping two smallest → nums[n−1]−nums[2]; drop two largest → nums[n−3]−nums[0]; drop one of each → nums[n−2]−nums[1]. Any other deletion of two elements leaves a superset-range of one of these three.
a.t: O(n log n) — dominated by sorting.
a.sp: O(1) — in-place sort (or O(n) depending on sort implementation).

a.n: Approach 2: One pass, O(n), no sort
a.i: Only the three smallest and three largest values matter. Track them in a single scan and apply the same three-candidate formula.
s: Scan once maintaining mins (three smallest) and maxs (three largest).
Evaluate the same three expressions using those six tracked values.
a.t: O(n) — single pass with constant work per element.

w: The crucial leap is realizing the low score can always be zeroed by duplicating a survivor, reducing the problem to minimizing the survivors' range.
